after: ## Methods and methodology: the working difference
alt: Three layers of a methods section: methods, what you did; procedure, how you did it; and methodology, why those methods suit this kind of question in this subject and what they allow you to conclude. Most weak methods sections stop at the first layer.
caption: Say what you did, how, and why it suits the question; most weak answers stop at what.

after: ## Step 1: work out what kind of question you have asked
alt: Four question types matched to evidence and methods. Empirical questions need measurement and suit data analysis, surveys or experiments; interpretive questions need close reading and suit text analysis or interviews; normative questions need arguments about values plus evidence of consequences; explanatory questions need evidence that tests competing explanations.
caption: The kind of question decides the evidence, and the evidence decides the method.

after: ## Step 3: design each method so it can be defended
alt: Six methods with their design decisions: a literature review needs a search strategy, inclusion rules and organisation by perspective; text analysis needs chosen passages and an alternative reading; interviews need participants, open questions and theme analysis; surveys need sampling and piloting; data need checked definitions; experiments need controlled variables and safety.
caption: Choosing a method is not enough; explain how you carried it out.

after: ## Step 4: combine methods where one is not enough
alt: National data shows that a change happened; interviews show how people experienced it. Comparing them gives two outcomes: if both point the same way the conclusion is more secure, and if they conflict the conflict is a finding to discuss. Two well-designed methods are usually more manageable than four thin ones.
caption: Mix methods so each answers what the other cannot, or checks it.

alt: Four ethical conventions for research involving people: informed consent, anonymity and confidentiality, the right to withdraw at any point, and sensitivity and safety for participants and the researcher.
caption: Show in the methods section how each convention was met.

alt: Five questions in order, each answered from the league-tables example: what was done, how exactly, why it suits the question and subject, what the limits are, and how those limits affect the conclusion.
caption: Name, describe, justify, limit, then apply the limit to the conclusion.

alt: Four kinds of evidence with what each can and cannot support: qualitative evidence from a few people shows how and why but not how common; data from one place supports conclusions about that place first; correlation does not establish cause alone; outcome evidence needs explicit reasoning about values to support a normative judgement.
caption: State the boundary your methods set, and keep your conclusion inside it.
